```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(fpp3)
library(BVAR)
```

## 1. ARIMA vs. ETS (PART 2)

#2.1a

```{r}
liquor_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/MRTSSM4453USN.csv",
  na = ".",
  col_types = cols(
    observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"),
    MRTSSM4453USN = col_double()
  )
)

liquor <- liquor_raw |>
  transmute(Month = yearmonth(observation_date), sales = MRTSSM4453USN) |>
  as_tsibble(index = Month) |>
  filter(Month <= yearmonth("2019 Dec"))

has_gaps(liquor)
```

#2.1b

```{r}
liquor |>
  gg_season(log(sales)) +
  labs(
    title = "Seasonal Pattern of Log Liquor Store Sales",
    x = "Month",
    y = "Log(Sales)"
  )
```

#Answer to 2.1b\
Generally upward trend, liquor sales seem to increase overtime. Sales dip starting in January to February with a noticible dip in September, possibly due to school starting. Summer months, especially July seem to have some of the highest sales with a noticible peak in May as well. I'd say the swings are pretty stable across the years. This means that using logs works well because it helps make the seasonal trend more stable with it's varience.

#2.2a

```{r}
liquor_fit <- liquor |>
  model(arima = ARIMA(log(sales)),
        ets   = ETS(log(sales)))

liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> report()

liquor_fit |> select(ets) |> report()
```

#2.2a Answer: \
ARIMA(1,0,2)(2,1,1)\[12\] w/ drift \# meaning one nonseasonal autoregressive, zero nonseasonal differencing, two nonseasonal moving-average, two seasonal autoregressive, one seasonal difference, and one seasonal moving-average term.\
ETS(A,A,A) meaning additive error, additive trend, and additive seasonality. Its all ADDICTIVE. \
\
#2.2b

```{r}
liquor_fit |> select(arima) |> gg_tsresiduals()

liquor_fit |>
  select(arima) |>
  augment() |>
  features(.innov, ljung_box, lag = 24, dof = 6)
```

#Answer to 2.2b: They do not look like white noise, they have an appromately normal bell curve.\
\
#2.3a

```{r}
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")
```

#Answer to 2.3a: Total of 336 months - 120 in the training sample - dropped final sample from December 2019 because of evil Covid-19 = 215

#2.3b

```{r}
liquor_cv_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_cv_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE))
```

#Answer to 2.3b: The first forecast was in Feburary 2002, and the last was January 2020. I would say ARIMA forecasted more accurately since it has a lower RMSE and MAE, which the metrics do agree on.\
\
#2.4

```{r}
#DM Test

liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets, h = 1, power = 2)

#ARIMA VS SNAIVE

liquor_errs <- liquor_cv_fc |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(as_tibble(liquor) |> select(Month, actual = sales),
            by = "Month") |>
  mutate(e = actual - .mean) |>
  select(Month, .model, e) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = .model, values_from = e)

forecast::dm.test(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$snaive,
                  h = 1, power = 2)
```

#Answer to 2.4: With a p value below 0.05, we reject the null hypothesis that both models forecast equally as accurate. ARIMA beat ETS and SNAIVE into the ground. If I owned the liquor chain, I'd use ARIMA since it beats the other two and has less forecast errors. \

## 2. Forecast Combination (PART 3)

3a:

```{r}
liquor_cv_fit <- readRDS("results/liquor_cv_fit.rds")

liquor_combo_fc <- liquor_cv_fit |>
  mutate(combo = (arima + ets) / 2) |>
  forecast(h = 1)

liquor_combo_fc |>
  accuracy(liquor, measures = list(RMSE = RMSE, MAE = MAE)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

Answer to 3a: The combo did better than ETS and the SNAIVE, but not ARIMA. This means ARIMA on its own is stronger. \
\
#3b

```{r}
cor(liquor_errs$arima, liquor_errs$ets)
```

Answer to 3b: The correlation given was 0.8782931, which is generally a strong positive relationship. This means ARIMA and ETS had a relationship between their errors, likely because they made similar errors so adding them together doesn't do much. We already saw in 2.4 that ARIMA solos, so it doesn't make sense to give them both equal weight.

## 3. VAR vs. BVAR (PART 4)

#4.1a:

```{r}
qd_raw <- read_csv("data/fredqd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  slice(-(1:2))
```

\
#4.1b:

```{r}
growth <- function(x) 100 * difference(log(x))

qd <- qd_raw |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y")) |>
  transmute(date,
            gdp    = growth(GDPC1),     # real GDP
            cons   = growth(PCECC96),   # real consumption
            inv    = growth(GPDIC1),    # real investment
            emp    = growth(PAYEMS),    # payroll employment
            infl   = growth(GDPCTPI),   # GDP price index
            unrate = difference(UNRATE),     # unemployment rate
            ffr    = difference(FEDFUNDS),   # federal funds rate
            gs10   = difference(GS10)) |>    # 10-year Treasury yield
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

y <- qd |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

nrow(y)
head(y)
```

\
#4.1c

```{r}
N <- nrow(y)
origins <- 120:(N - 1)
actual <- y[121:N, ]
```

#Answer to 4.1c: 240 quarters - 120 training sample quarters = 120. The first forecast was for Q1 of 1990, and the last Q4 of 2019.\

#4.2

```{r}
var_ols_fc <- function(z, p) {
  e <- embed(z, p + 1)
  M <- ncol(z)
  B <- coef(lm(e[, 1:M] ~ e[, -(1:M)]))
  x <- c(1, t(z[nrow(z):(nrow(z) - p + 1), ]))
  x %*% B
}

fc_var1 <- NULL
fc_var4 <- NULL

for (T in origins) {
  fc_var1 <- rbind(fc_var1, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 1))
  fc_var4 <- rbind(fc_var4, var_ols_fc(y[1:T, ], 4))
}

rmse_by_var <- function(f) sqrt(colMeans((actual - f)^2))

var_results_42 <- tibble(
  Variable = colnames(y),
  `VAR(1)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var1),
  `VAR(4)` = rmse_by_var(fc_var4)
)

var_results_42 |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

#Answer to 4.2: VAR(1) forecast seven out of 8, VAR(4) only winning for inflation. Because VAR(4) deals with more parameters, it increases the odds of errors through overfitting. This is why VAR(1) is superior. \
\
#4.3a and 4.3b:

```{r}
fc_bvar_03 <- readRDS("results/fc_bvar_03.rds")

var_results <- readRDS("results/var_results.rds")

var_results |> knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

#Answers to 4.3b:

1.  BVAR(4) has a lower RSME that the OLS VAR(4) for all eight of the variables. BVAR uses a Minnesota prior to shrink coefficents to reduce uncertainity, that's whats different.
2.  BVAR(4) does better for three variables specifcally, investment, inflation, and 10-year treasury rate but VAR(1) does better on the remaining 5.
3.  The forecasting seemed to be worse, telling me that shrinkage is too restritive. Well, the RSME was only the winner out of comparison and performance to other models, that's not certain for the future,

#4.3c:

```{r}
e_var4 <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_var4[, 1]
e_bvar <- actual[, "gdp"] - fc_bvar_03[, 1]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4, e_bvar, h = 1, power = 2)

#Choosing unemployment now

e_var4_unrate <- actual[, "unrate"] - fc_var4[, 6]
e_bvar_unrate <- actual[, "unrate"] - fc_bvar_03[, 6]

forecast::dm.test(e_var4_unrate, e_bvar_unrate, h = 1, power = 2)
```

Answer to 4.3c: GDP has a p value of 0.03468 while unemployment had a p value of 0.07592. This means GDP does better than VAR(4), but we cannot comment on unemployment at a signifcane level of 0.05. BVAR thus varies across different variables, so it doesn't mean its necesaarily always more accurate. \

## 4. Factor Model (PART 5)

#5.1a and 5.1b:

```{r}
md_raw <- read_csv("data/fredmd_2026-09.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

tcode <- unlist(md_raw[1, -1])

md <- md_raw[-1, ] |>
  mutate(date = as.Date(sasdate, "%m/%d/%Y"))

transform_series <- function(x, code) {
  d <- function(v) c(NA, diff(v))
  switch(as.character(code),
         "1" = x,
         "2" = d(x),
         "3" = d(d(x)),
         "4" = log(x),
         "5" = 100 * d(log(x)),
         "6" = 100 * d(d(log(x))),
         "7" = d(x / dplyr::lag(x) - 1))
}

fm <- map2_dfc(md[names(tcode)], tcode, transform_series) |>
  mutate(date = md$date, .before = 1) |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"),
         date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))

fm <- fm[, colSums(is.na(fm)) == 0]

dim(fm)
```

\
#5.1c:

```{r}
tcode[c("INDPRO", "PAYEMS", "CPIAUCSL", "FEDFUNDS")]
```

#Answer to 5.1c: \
INDPRO, percentage growth in industrail production via 100 x the first logged difference.

PAYEMS, percentage growth in employment via 100 x the first logged difference.

CPIAUCSL, change in the inflation rate via 100 x the second logged difference.

FEDFUNDS, change in the federal funds interest rate via the first difference.

FEDFUNDS already uses a first difference w/ an interest rate as a percentage while INDPRO is the percent growth over time in the data. \

```{r}
Z <- fm |> select(-date) |> as.matrix()

pc <- prcomp(scale(Z))

summary(pc)$importance[, 1:5]
```

#5.3:

```{r}
ip <- fm$INDPRO
n <- nrow(Z)
init <- which(fm$date == as.Date("1989-12-01"))

e_ar <- NULL
e_fa <- NULL
for (T in init:(n - 1)) {
  F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:3]         # factors using data through T
  d <- data.frame(y_next = ip[2:T], y = ip[1:(T - 1)], F_T[1:(T - 1), ])
  new <- data.frame(y = ip[T], t(F_T[T, ]))
  e_ar <- c(e_ar, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ y, d), new))
  e_fa <- c(e_fa, ip[T + 1] - predict(lm(y_next ~ ., d), new))
}

c(RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)))
```

#Answer to 5.3: Numbers confirmed! o7. This is cheating because your are looking ahead at data, which will influence results. In the real world this wouldn't work, unless you can time travel. \
\
\
#5.4

```{r}
direct_race <- function(series, h = 12, r = 3) {
  lv <- md |>
    mutate(log_x = log(.data[[series]]),
           g = 100 * (log_x - lag(log_x))) |>
    filter(date >= as.Date("1960-03-01"), date <= as.Date("2019-12-01"))
  yh <- 100 * (lead(lv$log_x, h) - lv$log_x)      # growth over the next h months
  g  <- lv$g                                      # growth over the latest month
  
  e_ar <- NULL
  e_fa <- NULL
  for (T in init:(n - h)) {
    F_T <- prcomp(scale(Z[1:T, ]))$x[, 1:r, drop = FALSE]
    i <- 1:(T - h)
    d <- data.frame(yh = yh[i], g = g[i], F_T[i, , drop = FALSE])
    new <- data.frame(g = g[T], F_T[T, , drop = FALSE])
    e_ar <- c(e_ar, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ g, d), new))
    e_fa <- c(e_fa, yh[T] - predict(lm(yh ~ ., d), new))
  }
  tibble(series, forecasts = length(e_ar),
         RMSE_AR = sqrt(mean(e_ar^2)), RMSE_FA = sqrt(mean(e_fa^2)),
         MAE_AR = mean(abs(e_ar)), MAE_FA = mean(abs(e_fa)),
         DM_pvalue = forecast::dm.test(e_ar, e_fa, h = h, power = 2,
                                       varestimator = "bartlett")$p.value)
}

direct_race("CPIAUCSL")
```

#Answer to 5.4: The factors do improve the forecast, since the AR model had an RSME of 2.11 (rounded) and the augmented model had a 1.89 (rounded). (2.11-1.89) / 2.11 = 0.1042654028 x 100 = 10.43% (rounded). With a p value of 0.000443 from the DM test, it is significant at an alpha level of 0.01.

## 5. Reflection (PART 6)

#Reflection: As we combined models and varied complexity, it became clear that complexity was not always the winner. When it came to the solo ARIMA model vs a combined model, the ARIMA still out performed. Combinations at times didn't always offer better results, and different variables were not always consitent. Likely, complexity in parameters can just add more risk in accuracy compared to a well performing single model. In the end models vary in results based on weight, fit, and complexity.
